purpose: This medication is a numbing cream or patch applied to the skin to reduce pain before certain medical procedures, like blood draws, IV placement, or minor skin treatments. It helps make the skin feel numb so you experience less discomfort during the procedure. It is only for use on the skin and is not swallowed.
how_it_works: Lidocaine and tetracaine both belong to a group of medicines called local anesthetics. They work by temporarily blocking the nerve signals in the area where they are applied, so your nerves cannot send pain messages to your brain. Think of it like putting your skin on pause — the feeling comes back after the medicine wears off.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects happen right where the medicine is applied and include redness, paleness, swelling, or mild irritation of the skin. You might also notice a brief burning or itching sensation when it is first applied. These effects are usually mild and go away on their own.
warnings: Do not use this on broken, irritated, or damaged skin, or near your eyes or mouth unless your doctor specifically tells you to. Using too much or leaving it on longer than directed can cause serious problems, including dizziness, irregular heartbeat, or seizures from too much medicine being absorbed into your body. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, breastfeeding, or taking other medicines, especially other numbing medicines or heart medicines.
typical_dosing: For the cream form, a thick layer is usually applied to the skin and left on for 20 to 60 minutes before your procedure, then wiped off. For the patch form, it is applied to the skin about 20 to 30 minutes before the procedure. Always follow your doctor or nurse's exact instructions, since the amount and timing can vary depending on the procedure.
